results.content: # 3 Statistical Models for Causal Inference in ML Algorithms. 3 Statistical Models for Causal Inference in ML Algorithms. In this article, we explore three statistical models—Bayesian Networks, Structural Causal Models, and the Potential Outcomes Framework—that integrate causal inference in ML. 2. **Structural Causal Models (SCMs):** Offering a more rigorous theoretical framework, SCMs integrate mathematical equations and graph theory to represent causal structures. 3. **Potential Outcomes Framework:** Also known as the Rubin Causal Model, this approach focuses on treatment effects and is widely used in experimental and observational studies. Each model brings its own advantages and challenges to ML, and understanding these differences can guide the selection and integration of causal models for real-world applications. Overall, the Bayesian Network framework serves as a robust starting point for integrating causal inference in ML due to its balance of theoretical elegance and practical applicability. Structural Causal Models (SCMs) extend beyond the scope of Bayesian Networks by offering a framework that combines graph theory with a set of structural equations. The Potential Outcomes Framework, also known as the Rubin Causal Model, is widely used in the evaluation of treatment effects and randomized experiments. Despite these caveats, the Potential Outcomes Framework remains a cornerstone in causal analysis, providing useful insights into the effects of interventions, particularly when combined with modern ML techniques. ## Integrating Causal Models in ML. Clearly specify the causal model structure, be it a Bayesian Network, SCM, or potential outcomes framework. Once the causal model is validated, integrate it into existing ML pipelines to enhance decision-making. In this article, we explored three prominent statistical models used for causal inference in ML:. * **Structural Causal Models (SCMs):** Offer a rigorous method for modeling interventions, integrating both graph theory and structural equations to analyze cause-and-effect. Whether you’re a data scientist looking to improve model performance or a policymaker striving to make evidence-based decisions, integrating causal inference into your ML toolkit is a valuable investment. By harnessing the power of these three models—Bayesian Networks, Structural Causal Models, and the Potential Outcomes Framework—ML practitioners can elevate their algorithms from mere predictive tools to platforms that offer deep insights into the underlying forces shaping our world.

results.title: Bayesian networks and causal inference
results.content:
Title: Bayesian networks and causal inference
# Bayesian networks and causal inference. The relationships between even a small number of random variables can be quite confusing and possibly counter-intuitive. Two variables might be independent before observing the value of a third variable but dependent afterward. The opposite is true as well: two variables may be associated *a priori* but conditionally independent after observing third variable. Sequences of relationships between variables quickly become too complex to manage informally. Fortunately **Bayesian networks** provide a way to work effectively with interconnected sets of random variables. Bayesian networks let you visualize relationships between variables and guide calculations based on these variables. They are useful in modeling dependencies and carrying out calculations by hand involving a small number of variables. They also **scale up well**, allowing machine learning algorithms to work efficiently with hundreds or thousands of variables. Bayesian networks are also a useful tool for **causal reasoning**. Here one does not simply passively observe random variables but can also reason about the effects of intervening to set the states modeled by random variables using the so-called “do-calculus.” Causal reasoning also lets you reason rigorously about counterfactuals. Causal inference often makes it possible to carry out calculations that seem at first to be impossible, such as computing probabilities of outcomes in networks that include variables that have not and cannot be observed, such as hypothetical mediating causes. # The relation between Statistical Inference and Causal Inference. I found a number of excellent videos on this dispute about causal inference that should be of interest. ### Bayesian Causal Inference. ### Bayesian Causal Inference for Real World Interactive Systems. Bayesian Causal Inference for Real World Interactive Systems. **Larry Wasserman - Problems With Bayesian Causal Inference**. But he discusses how causal inference questions are more challenging from a computational POV than the more simple versions seen assessment of interventions. **Philip Dawid - Causal Inference Is Just Bayesian Decision Theory**. This is pretty much my intuition on the issue, but Dawid shows how causal inference problems are merely an instance of the more general Bayesian process and equivalent to Pearl’s DAGs.with the assumption of vast amounts of data. **Finnian Lattimore - Causal Inference with Bayes Rule**. Excellent discussion on how to do Bayesian (Causal) inference with finite data. I’m very sympathetic to her POV that causal inference isn’t all that different from “statistical” inference, but one participant (**Carlos Cinelli**) kept insisting there is some distinction between “causal inference” and decision theory applications. They seem to insist that modelling the relation among probability distributions is meta to the “statistical inference” process, while that step seems naturally part of it to a Bayesian. **Panel Discussion: Does causality mean we need to go beyond Bayesian decision theory?**. He calls the deductive process “logical” and in an effort to make Bayesian inference appear absurd, he concludes that “If logical deduction is Bayesian, everything is Bayesian inference.”. **Cinelli:** (Thinking he is scoring a debate point) But it is a physical model, not a statistical model…. Lattimore effectively refuted the Perlian distinction between “statistical inference” and “causal inference.” Does “statistical mechanics” cease to be part of physics because of the use of “statistical” models? The Perlian CGM school of thought essentially cannot conceive of the use of informative Bayesian inference, which physicists RT Cox and ET Jaynes advocated. **David Rohde - Causal Inference is Inference – A beautifully simple idea that not everyone accepts**. **Causal Inference with Bayes rule with Finnian Lattimore and David Rohde**. results.title: Bayesian inference is not what you think it is! | Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science
results.content: # Statistical Modeling, Causal Inference, and Social Science. # Bayesian inference is not what you think it is! Bayesian statistics means different things to different people. > “Bayesian inference uses aspects of the scientific method, which involves collecting evidence that is meant to be consistent or inconsistent with a given hypothesis. . proponents of Bayesian inference say that it can be used to discriminate between conflicting hypotheses: hypotheses with very high support should be accepted as true and those with very low support should be rejected as false.” — Wikipedia article on “Bayesian inference”. It may come as a surprise to some readers that this is not how I view Bayesian inference at all! In my work, I treat Bayesian methods as a souped-up least squares or maximum likelihood, a way to perform better inference within a model. For example, when modeling the rates of which New York City police stopped people of different ethnic groups (Gelman, Fagan, and Kiss, 2007), we did not attempt to compute the probability of the hypothesis that police stopped blacks, hispanics, and whites at the same rate; rather, we estimated these different probabilities and assessed how they varied for different types of crimes and in different parts of the city. In estimating social networks using survey data (Zheng, Salganik, and Gelman, 2006), we did not estimate our degree of belief in the hypothesis that people formed social ties at random; instead, we fit a model in which people varied in their social networks, and compared our fitted model to predictions from the simpler model. I’m not trying to argue that the Wikipedians’ interpretation is wrong, just that their view focuses on what seems to me to be a small part of what Bayesian statistics is about. What is relevant here–and, again, which I suspect will be a surprise to many readers who are not practicing applied statisticians–is that what is in Bayesian statistics textbooks is much different from what outsiders think is important about Bayesian inference, or Bayesian data analysis. Also relevant is our 2013 article on philosophy and the practice of Bayesian statistics. It’s a funny thing to be applying a method that otherwise well-informed people have such a misguided view about.
